doc.title: Ashley Keating and Allan Whitworth Interview, 1963-03-22

title: Individual members of the Gibson band
summary: Keating gives opinions on Eddie Richardson, the trombonist, Dave Bailey and the trumpeters Sonny Williams and John Wimbley.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: No, I don't mind. Uh, well, as regards, uh, this is the Gibson band you're talking about. Yeah, the Gibson band. Yes. Uh, I was, I was impressed with, uh, Eddie Richardson to start with. Uh, he's the leader. I think he behaves as though he is. Yeah, he's the musical director. He's the, yes, that, uh, I, I would say he would be, by far the best musician. Uh, the trombonist, Carol Blunt, uh, also impressed. I don't know how he'd be in a jazz band, but he certainly did know how to drive it down in a, in a marching band. Uh, the Althaus seemed to, uh, to add a little tonal coloring with, uh, various out of tune phrases. Uh, but it still seemed to add to the charm of the music somehow. Uh, uh, Dave Bailey too. He was a bit. Uh, on his bass drum and cymbal. Uh, I think they were the outstanding members of the band. Uh, the second trumpeter who arrived later, I've forgotten his name. Well, first it was Sonny Williams, who, that's right. The older man, and rather soft, and that's funny. Yes,

And then, then the other one arrived later was John Wimbley. That's right. Yes, well, uh, he seemed to have, uh, a particularly good idea of playing second trumpet to me. Mm-hmm. Although from what I've, uh, read on Barry Martin records, et cetera, uh, Eddie Richardson is, uh, allegedly an ideal second trumpet. Uh, but Eddie Richardson to me seemed to be very powerful, and, in, in particularly good lip.

When he was with the Eureka, he's the guy who carried the melody with him, you know. Yeah. Not, not second trumpet. No, he, and with this he's, man, he's more featured. That's right. Yeah, so it would appear that way. Yeah, well, they have, uh, a funny kind of setup in the New Orleans brass band trumpet. There's no point in going into that now. Uh, let's see. What did you think of the, uh, alto player who arrived later, Earl Batiste?
